input:
The three-month pilot on 22 pumps should proceed, at a cost of $38k, and the decision on full installation should be held until the pilot results are reported. The pilot is owned by the reliability engineering group, which reports before the March capital review.

The base is the plant's own record. Across 180 pumps, maintenance records for 12 months show 969 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 38% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $443k installed, plus $63k per year: the full commitment is large against a benefit that has not been measured at this plant. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 19%; the figure is a vendor figure, and it is the only performance figure in the case.

The pilot buys the missing measurement. Run on 22 pumps over three months, it tests the sensors on the plant's own pumps, under the plant's own operating pattern, and returns a downtime figure the full decision can rest on. The trade stands in one sentence: $38k and one reporting cycle, against a commitment of $443k plus $63k per year taken on a vendor's number. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, and the pilot does not disturb that position: a bearing failure detected early is still a bearing failure awaited on the same lead time, and no part of the case rests on spares.

The recommendation is therefore bounded. The pilot proceeds; full installation is neither approved nor refused, and it returns to the March capital review with the pilot results in hand.
